sections.heading: ABSTRACT
sections.text:
Electrochemical carbon dioxide reduction reaction (CO2RR) is a promising solution to the current
environmental and energy issues. Cu is the only metal catalyst able to convert CO2 into high value-
added hydrocarbons. However, Cu catalysts tend to degrade with the decrease in the hydrocarbon
selectivity under operation condition. Herein we monitored the morphological evolution of Cu
nanocatalysts and correlated with changes in the selectivity of hydrocarbon products during
electrochemical CO2 reduction. Initial Cu nanospheres quickly reconstructed into nanocubes
within 1-hour CO2 electrolysis, and then gradually turned into even smaller irregular nanoparticles.
Interestingly, the above unstable Cu nanocube offered the maximum ethylene selectivity. We
successfully stabilized these Cu nanocubes using 2D graphene surface doped with nitrogen to
achieve a high ethylene selectivity over 24 hours. Our X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS)
and density-functional theory (DFT) investigations show that the strong interaction between Cu
and pyridinic nitrogen on the 2D graphene surface plays a key role in stabilizing Cu nanocubes.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
Fossil fuel consumption is increasing our concerns about the environmental issues and energy
crisis.1, 2 Electrochemical carbon dioxide reduction reaction (CO2RR) is one of the most promising
ways to solve these problems.3-7 It could be combined with solar energy to convert CO2 to carbon-
neutral fuels or industrial chemicals, which is very important for humans to meet the needs of long-
term global sustainability.8-11 Over the past several decades, the focus has been on the investigation
of Cu-based catalysts,12-14 since copper is only known material that can catalyze CO2 to various
hydrocarbon products, such as ethanol, ethylene, methane and so on.1, 15-17 To obtain a specific
product with high selectivity from CO2RR, significant efforts have been devoted to investigate the
effects of morphologies, defects, unsaturated-atoms of nanostructured catalysts and bimetal
catalysts.18-26 For example , Cu (100) is highly selective to C2H4, while Cu (111) is highly selective
to CH4. 27-32 It has been reported that Cu cubes mainly exposed with (100) facets which can
selectively convert CO2 to C2H4. 33, 34
For practical use, long-term stability is a key parameter beyond selectivity and activity.35
Osowiecki et al. reported that during CO2RR, the Cu nanoparticles tended to change into larger
Cu nanocubes and then de-cluster to small irregular Cu nanoparticles.36 Grosse et al. found that
drastic morphological changes of Cu nanocubes took place under CO2RR, which led to the
suppression of the selectivity of C2H4 over CH4. 37 Huang et al. reported that most Cu nanocubes
evolved into smaller and rounded particles due to a rapid detachment of nanoclusters from Cu
nanocubes under operation conditions. This results in an improvement in the faradaic efficiency
(FE) towards hydrogen evolution (HER) side reaction instead of CO2RR. , which is consistent with
previous findings that smaller Cu nanoparticles and nanoclusters with a higher number of low-
coordination sites prefer HER.38 Therefore it is crucial to stabilize the structure of Cu nanocubes

for high ethylene selectivity.39, 40 However, there are few reports on methods for maintaining the
structure of reconstructed ethylene-selective Cu nanocubes.
In the present work, we first investigated the morphological evolution of Cu nanocatalysts
and analyzed the change in selectivity of hydrocarbon products during electrochemical CO2
reduction. Then we developed a simple method to prepare monodisperse Cu NPs on N-doped two-
dimensional (2D) graphene oxide, which prevents Cu nanocubes to break apart and achieves a
high ethylene selectivity of more than 30% over 24 hours. DFT investigations show that the strong
interaction between Cu and pyridinic nitrogen on the 2D graphene surface plays a key role in
stabilizing above Cu nanocubes. Thus, we have presented an efficient strategy to anchor Cu
nanocubes with nitrogen-doped graphene oxide and to achieve a stable ethylene selectivity.

sections.heading: Experimental Section
sections.text:
Materials Graphene oxide (XFNANO, INC), Cupric chloride (CuCl2, Aladdin, 98%), Cupric
acetate (Cu(OAc)2, Kermel, 98%), Sodium borohydride (NaBH4, Alfa, 98%), Sodium citrate
(Na3C6H5O7· 2H2O, Kermel, 99%), Sodium hydroxide (NaOH, Kermel, 96%), Hydrazine
hydrate (H6N2O, Aladdin, 80%), Aqueous ammonia (NH3, Kermel, 28%), Ethanol (C2H5OH,
Kermel, 99.7%), isopropyl alcohol (C3H7OH, Kemel, 99.7%), Deionized water (Kermel). All
materials of analytical grade and were used without further purification.
Synthesis of Cu catalysts Cu nanocrystals were synthesized using a modified method reported in our previous studies.41 Firstly, 750μL of 0.1M sodium citrate drop was added to CuCl2 solution in
the three neck flask using micropipettes. Then, 10mL of graphene oxide dispersion drop was also
added into the solution and stirred for 0.5h. After adding the support, NaBH4 was added into the
solution and stirred under an argon atmosphere and ice-bath. After 2hrs of reaction, the production
was collected by vacuum suction filtration and dried in the vacuum drier at 90℃ for 4h.
Synthesis of N-doped graphene oxide The N-doped graphene oxide was synthesized according to a literature procedure.42 First, 5 mL of aqueous ammonia was added into 20mL of Graphene
oxide. Then, the solution was sonicated at room temperature for 3hrs. The precipitate was collected
by centrifugation, washed with the mixture of 25mL deionized water and 50mL ethanol for 3 times,
and dried at 45℃ overnight.
Synthesis of Cu nanocubes First, 184mL of deionized water was added into a radius flask which
was previously dried and stirred and heated in water-bath at 50℃ until the temperature does not
change. Then, 2mL 0.1M Cu(OAc)2, 10mL nitrogen-doped graphene oxide solution (sonicated
with 5mL isopropyl alcohol and 5mL deionized water), 2mL 0.1M NaOH and 0.1M Hydrazine
hydrate (H6N2O) were added in sequence every 3 mins. After stirring for 2hrs, the production was
collected by vacuum suction filtration and dried in the vacuum drier at 80℃ for 0.5h.
Physical Characterization Cu/GO catalysts were characterized by TEM (Jem-2100f) and X-ray
powder diffraction (XRD, Bruker D8). The scans of XRD were collected from 10 to 90 degrees at
a scanning rate of 5 degrees per minute. N 1s spectra of the samples were collected using X-ray
photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) which instrument is K-Alpha+ and produced by ThermoFisher
in the UK. It takes Al Ka as the X-ray source and calibrates the binding energy with the emission C1s (calibration value: 284.8), and the vacuum condition is 5*10-8 Pa.

Electrolysis The electrochemical CO2 reduction was carried out using an H-type, 3-electrode cell,
using the Cu/GO catalyst as the working electrode, the Ag/AgCl is used as reference electrode and
platinum plate electrode as the counter electrode, respectively. The three electrodes were immersed
in the aqueous solution of 0.1 M KHCO3 as the electrolytes. To avoid formic acid oxidation by Pt
counter electrode, a proton exchange membrane was used to separate cathode and anode areas.
The electrochemical measurements were performed out under the control of an electrochemical
work station. CO2 was constantly bubbled into the electrolyte to maintain CO2 saturated
environment and gaseous products such as CO, CH4, C2H4, C2H6 and H2, produced at the cathode
were delivered to the online gas chromatograph (GC-2014C SHIMADZU CAS
CHROMATOGRAPH) for the analysis. The CO2 flow rate was set to 20 sccm, which was
controlled by a mass flow controller. Liquid products were collected from the cathode chamber
after electrolysis. Theresults were analyzed by nuclear magnetic resonance (AVANCE IIITM HD
400 MHz NanoBAY, Bruker).
Theoretical calculations The spin-polarized calculations have been carried out in the density
functional theory (DFT) framework as implemented in the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP).43 The ion-electron interactions are represented by the projector-augmented wave (PAW) method44 and the electron exchange-correlation by the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) with the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) exchange-correlation functional.45 The Kohn-Sham
valence states were expanded in a plane-wave basis with a cut-off energy of 400 eV. The Cu(3d4s),
N(2s2p), O(2s2p), and C(2s2p) electrons were treated as valence states.
For graphene monolayer, the models were a periodic slab with a (3×3) surface supercell
containing 18 carbon atoms. In the case of graphene oxide (GO), 9 oxygen atoms were evenly
loaded on graphene monolayer. For nitrogen-doped graphene, the N3OV4 model have been
adopted, with four carbon vacancies and three nitrogen atoms bound to carbon vacancies. The
thickness of the vacuum slab is 15 Å. The integration of the Brillouin-zone wes performed by
using a (9×9×1) Monkhorst-Pack mesh during optimization. The iterative process considered as convergences, when the force on the atom was < 0.02 eV Å−1 and the energy change was <10–5 eV
per atom. The adsorption energy of the copper atom on supports is calculated by
Eads = ECu-sup – (ECu + Esup) (1)
Where ECu and Esup are the energies of a free copper atom and supports (graphene, GO and
N-doped graphene), respectively. ECu-sup is the energy of complex of Cu adsorbed on supports.

sections.heading: Results and Discussion
sections.text:
Material synthesis and CO2RR performance
We first synthesized ultrafine Cu nanocrystals using sodium citrate as a stabilizer. The
following factors were found to be crucial for the effective synthesis of highly dispersed Cu
nanocrystals on the carbon support. First, surface chemistry of supports could significantly affect
the dispersion of Cu nanocrystals. Due to the lack of defects and unsaturated atoms of carbon black
support, Cu nanocrystals seriously agglomerated on its surface (Figure S1, Supporting
Information). In contrast, 2D graphene oxide with a high surface area and abundant oxygen-
containing groups46 promoted the dispersion of Cu nanocrystals. Second, fresh NaBH4 aqueous
solution is employed to reduce Cu2+ precursors under an ice-bath and argon atmosphere. The ice-
bath is designed to stabilize NaBH4, making it less likely to react with water, while the argon
atmosphere is used to prevent the Cu nanoparticles from being oxidized in air.
X-ray diffraction patterns (XRD) of various densities of Cu nanoparticles (NPs) on graphene
oxide are shown in Figure 1d. Three well-defined diffraction peaks at 2θ ≈ 43.2º, 50.4º and 74.1º
could be attributed to the Cu (111), (200) and (220) planes (PDF: 04-0836), respectively.
Furthermore, the intensity of these peaks increases with Cu NPs loadings. The transmission
electron microscope (TEM) images of Cu NPs on graphene oxide are shown in Figure 1. Most of
Cu NPs are isolated at the low loadings, which shows that an almost monodisperse spherical
morphology with a mean particle size of ca. 3.3 nm at 20 wt.% loading (Figure 1a), and approx.
ca. 3.8 nm at 40 wt.% loading (Figure 1b). In contrast, Cu NPs started to pack on GO (Figure 1c)
at the loading of 60 wt.% and heavily aggregated at the high loading of 80 wt.% (Figure S2 g, h).

gas chromatograph (GC) and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) analysis (Figure 1e), the faradaic

peak, which indicates the formation of Cu nanocubes, which is consistent with previous reports
that (100) facets on Cu nanocubes favor the generation of C2H4. 33 Therefore the maximum C2H4
selectivity was reached at the catalyst with 60 wt. % Cu loading.

The 60 wt. % Cu/GO catalyst demonstrated the best CO2RR performance among the above
samples. For practical use, long-term stability is a key parameter beyond selectivity and activity.
Next we investigated the stability of 60 wt. % Cu/GO catalyst at -1 V vs. RHE in CO2 saturated in
0.1M KHCO3. The initial faradaic efficiency of C2H4 was 27% but it quickly dropped to 6% within
24h reaction, while the selectivity of CO and H2 showed an obvious increase (Figure 2c). As
observed in TEM images of Figures 2a and 2b, the Cu NPs experienced a structural transformation
process from spherical to cube-like shape within the first 1 h electrolysis, consistent with the recent
research.47 This structural change increases the edge active sites and defects on the surface of Cu
NPs, which enhances the selectivity to C2H4. 48-50 However, the cube-like structure could not be
maintained for a long time. As shown in Figure 2b, within 24 h reaction, the Cu NPs changed from
cube-like morphology to some small and irregular nanoparticles, where they underwent a pitting
process and generated tiny pinholes at edges. As the CO2 electrolysis continues, each pinhole
serves as a new pitting center, and the framework of Cu nanocubes gradually collapses.38 Although
the partial current densities of ethylene on Cu/GO decreased with time due to the morphology
evolution during CO2 electrolysis (Figure S7), the increase in partial current densities of CO and
H2 could compensate and result in relatively stable total current densities (Figure S6).

sections.heading: Stability improvement strategy
sections.text:
To achieve stable CO2 electroreduction to ethylene, it is crucial to maintain the cubic structure
of Cu catalysts. To this end, we employed a simple wet-chemical method for the synthesis of
nitrogen doped graphene oxide (NGO) to support Cu nanocubes, where the strong interaction
between Cu NPs and doped nitrogen species on the 2D graphene surface is expected to stabilize
the cubic structure of Cu NPs (Figure 3d). As shown in Figure S7, excellent long-term stability of
Cu/NGO was demonstrated using 24 h electrolysis at -1 V and a stable C2H4 partial current density

was obtained during the electrolysis process. Moreover, as shown in Figure 3e, the cubic structure
of Cu NPs on NGOs could be almost maintained after 24 h electrolysis, and the faradaic efficiency
(%) of C2H4 was only reduced by a small number after a long time reaction (Figure 3f). In contrast,
Cu nanocubes supported on 2D graphene oxide (GO) without doped nitrogen gradually degraded
to small irregular Cu nanoparticles within the same period, which results in the significant decrease
in ethylene selectivity by about 50% (Figure 3b).

We then conducted XPS analysis to understand the nature of the strong interaction between the
nitrogen species and Cu.51, 52 The content of nitrogen in NGO determined by XPS is 6.3 at. %, and
does not change after Cu loading. According to the high-resolution XPS spectra of N 1s spectra of
NGO and Cu/NGO (Figure 4b), four peaks were observed, which correspond to pyridinic (N1,
398.2 eV), pyrrolic (N2, 399.8 eV), graphitic nitrogen (N3, 400.9 eV) and oxidized nitrogen
species (402.4 eV). After Cu was loaded on N doped graphene oxide, a new peak appeared at 399.0
eV of the N 1s spectra of Cu/NGO, while pyridinic nitrogen species were suppressed. The
appearance of the new peak at 399.0 eV and the decreased peak of pyridinic species originates
from the strong electronic interaction of Cu with pyridinic nitrogen sites.53 In addition, there is a
difference in the Cu2+ binding energies between Cu/N-GO and Cu/GO. As shown in Figure 4c, a
new peak appeared at 935.2 eV in the Cu 2p spectra of Cu/NGO. According to previous studies,
the binding energy for the Cu 2p3/2 line at 935.0-935.4 eV was assigned to Cu 2+ ions coordinated
by N-species.54, 55 Therefore, the stabilization of the Cu nanocubes on N-doped graphene oxide
could be attributed to the strong interaction between Cu and pyridinic nitrogen on NGO.

sections.heading: DFT calculations
sections.text:
DFT calculations were also carried out to elucidate the enhanced stability of Cu nanocubes
on the 2D graphene surface. We run spin-polarized calculations within the density functional
theory (DFT) framework as implemented in the Vienna ab initio simulation package (VASP). To
this end, Cu was performed on three graphene models: Cu on graphene (Figure 5a), Cu on graphene
oxide (Figure 5b), and Cu on N-doped graphene (Figure 5c). The calculated adsorption energies
of Cu on the three types of surfaces (graphene, graphene oxide and N-doped graphene) are -0.44,
-2.63 and -3.24 eV, respectively (Figure 5). N-doped graphene shows the strongest adsorption
energy to Cu, which again confirms the strong interaction between Cu and pyridinic nitrogen atoms.
Figure 5. A model of (a) Cu on graphene, (b) Cu on graphene oxide, and (c) Cu on N-doped graphene. The grey
color indicates C, brown for Cu, red for O, and blue for N.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text:
In summary, the reconstruction of Cu nanoparticles from spheres to cubes was observed
during electrochemical CO2 reduction, which significantly increased the selectivity of C2H4. Due
to the weak bond between Cu NPs and graphene oxide surface, these Cu nanocubes were not stable

and gradually broke into small and irregular nanoparticles, resulting in the reduced selectivity of
C2H4. To achieve a stable and high selectivity of C2H4, we employed 2D graphene doped with
nitrogen to anchor Cu nanocubes, which could be attributed to the strong interaction between Cu
NPs and pyridinic nitrogen atoms on the 2D graphene surface. This work provides an efficient
method for stabilizing Cu nanocubes by using N-doped 2D graphene oxide, which will benefit
their long term stability in practical applications.
